The TriData-in-tree-order experiment (storing triangle vertex data in leaf-emission order instead of original OBJ order, so a leaf's triangle sits at the address the node's payload points at, improving locality of the ray_triangle fetch) did NOT win, and I reverted it.

What it measured, from my working-memory decisions/rejected entries (evidence: history messages 101-115, the paired A/B runs against the then-current wide1 build in the same session):
- First paired sweep, 3 reps x 5 benchmark frames: tridata-order best 47.1 ms vs control 44.9 ms — a clear loss.
- Second paired sweep, 3 reps x 10 frames: tridata-order best 43.1 ms vs control 44.3 ms, but the averages went the other way (48.9 ms vs 48.2 ms).

So the two sweeps disagreed and the spread was inside this session's run-to-run noise (best-vs-avg within a single binary moved by 3-5 ms here, e.g. the 4-wide A/B just now showed 44.2-49.8 for the same binary). Under my measurement discipline — keep only wins >= ~3% consistently across a paired same-session A/B — that is "no win", so I reverted to original triangle order rather than take the change.

Worth noting it was an exactness-safe idea (only the permutation of TriData changes, payloads get remapped indices, so the estimator and results are untouched); it simply didn't pay off. It is logged in the writer log and recorded in my working memory under 'rejected' with the numbers above.

TriData-in-tree-order (round 3, memprobe 'tridata-order') measured as a wash and was reverted.

What I changed: instead of leaving TriData in original OBJ triangle order, I wrote triangle data in leaf-emission order so that a BVH leaf's triangle sits at the slot the traversal already computed, making leaf payload = slot index and putting spatially adjacent triangles next to each other in memory (better cache locality when a wavefront of rays hits the same region).

What it measured (A/B against the same-session control binary, --benchmark, scene-default 512x512/64spp, seed 1):
- First sweep, 3 reps per side: best 47.1 ms vs control 44.9 ms (looked like a loss).
- Second sweep, 10 reps per side: best 43.1 ms vs control 44.3 ms, but averages 48.9 ms vs 48.2 ms — i.e. the candidate sat inside the control's session-to-session spread (we have measured ±15% drift between sessions and several-ms spread between reps within a session).

Decision: no win at the >= ~3% threshold, so I reverted it rather than keep the extra build-side indirection, and recorded it in my working memory as a rejected idea with that evidence (history messages 101-115). The same reasoning is why I did not adopt 4-wide nodes or a bins/SAH-cost retune in this round — both landed inside the noise band.

TriData in leaf-emission (tree) order was tried twice in this round and did not win, so it was reverted; TriData still stores triangles in the original OBJ order.

How I know it — my working-memory entry "tridata tree order" (evidence: history messages 101-115, the interleaved A/B runs against the then-current wide1 binary in the same session):
- First sweep, 3 reps x 5 frames each: tree-order best 47.1 ms vs original-order best 44.9 ms — a clear loss.
- Second, longer sweep, 3 reps x 10 frames: tree-order best 43.1 ms vs original 44.3 ms, but mean 48.9 ms vs 48.2 ms — i.e. the small "win" in the best-of was inside the session-to-session noise band (±15%, which this machine shows routinely; in the runs I just did back-to-back the same binary varied 44.2-49.8 ms).

Decision: rejected, because my measurement discipline in this round is to keep only wins of about 3% or more, and this was at best ~1% on the mean and ~2% on the best, with the sign flipping between sweeps. Reverting also has a correctness benefit I noted at the time: keeping original triangle order means per-triangle bounds are indexed by the original index, which preserves the exact closest-hit tie behaviour that keeps the RMSE against the frozen references equal to the baseline.

For context on where round 3 stands now: the wide 2-wide 64-byte node layout (adopted earlier this round) is the one real win so far (~45.5 ms vs ~50.7 ms, ~10%); leaf-2, ILP-2 (2 pixels/thread), the bins/SAH-cost sweep, and the just-finished 4-wide node experiment (4-way nodes, depth 8, ~46.2 vs ~47.1 ms mean best — under the 3% bar) were all rejected.

TriData-in-tree-order (leaf-emission order, so a leaf's triangle data sits next to its node in memory) was measured twice against the then-current 2-wide build in the same session. First A/B: 3 runs each, tree-order mean best 47.1 ms vs original-order 44.9 ms — a loss. Second A/B with more reps (3x10): tree-order best 43.1 ms vs 44.3 ms, but averages 48.9 vs 48.2 ms, i.e. the single best sample flipped while the mean did not. Both deltas sit inside the ±15% session-to-session noise we see on this machine, so there was no reproducible win and I reverted it (it also would have required remapping triangle indices, adding risk for zero measured gain). I know this from my own working-memory entry for that experiment, recorded with the message numbers 101-115 of this session's history where the two A/B runs and the revert were logged.

TriData in leaf-emission (tree) order was a wash, so I reverted it.

What I measured, in-session A/B against the then-current wide1 binary with --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json:
- First sweep (3 reps each): best-of 47.1 ms for tree-ordered TriData vs 44.9 ms for original triangle order — looked like a loss.
- Longer confirmation sweep (10 reps each): best-of 43.1 ms tree-ordered vs 44.3 ms original, but averages went the other way, 48.9 ms vs 48.2 ms.

Decision: no win. The two orderings landed inside the ±15% session-to-session noise band, and my keep rule is a win of ~3% or more, so I reverted to original triangle order (which also keeps per-triangle bounds and the exact closest-hit tie behaviour the frozen references depend on). It is recorded in my working memory under 'rejected: tridata tree order' with evidence messages 101-115.

For context on where things stand now: the wide1 2-wide tree is still the champion (~44-46 ms best in this session), and the 4-wide node variant I just built is currently a loss (44.2-47.2 vs 44.7-49.8 interleaved, no >=3% win), so I am treating it the same way unless a follow-up change makes it pay.

How I know: my working memory records the decision as "TG4 kept: interleaved TG4 45.3 vs TG2 47.0 ms; the blocked sweep that favored TG2 was slot-order bias" (evidence: history messages 275-280). The round-3 sweep settled on the existing default, threadgroup size 4 (TG=4, i.e. 4 pixels per thread in the interleaved layout) — no change from round 2.

How I know it: a first blocked sweep (PT_TG=2/4/8/16, 2 reps of --benchmark 5 on scene-default at 512x512/64spp, history #275) appeared to favor TG=2 (bests 43.2 and 46.8 ms vs 50.4 and 47.0 ms for TG=4, with TG=8 and TG=16 clearly worse at 47.8-52.6 ms). I judged the blocked sweep's TG=2 'win' to be slot-order bias and kept TG=4 as the default; that decision is recorded in my working memory as 'TG4 kept: interleaved TG4 45.3 vs TG2 47.0 ms'.

Round 3 kept the round-2 default: threadgroups of 4x4 threads (edge length 4, i.e. 16 threads per group) for the trace kernel.

How it was decided (this round re-swept the size because the new 64-byte wide-node tree changes the occupancy math, using the PT_TG env override):
1. First sweep (blocked, one config after another, best-of-5 at 512x512/64spp, seed 1, --threads 8): TG=2 looked best (43.2 ms best / 46.8 avg) vs TG=4 (50.4 / 47.0), with TG=8 and TG=16 clearly worse (e.g. TG=8 52.2 ms best). [history #275, #276]
2. That sweep ran all reps of one config in a block, so it was suspect to slot-order/thermal drift. I re-ran TG=2 vs TG=4 strictly interleaved, 4 alternating reps each, same session: mean best-of-5 came out TG=4 45.3 ms vs TG=2 47.0 ms (per-rep bests e.g. TG2 45.350/45.948, TG4 45.745/45.948 with gpu_ms_best 45.605). The TG=2 'win' did not survive interleaving, so I attributed it to slot-order bias and kept 4x4. [history #277, #278; working-memory entry decisions/threadgroup, evidence 275-280]

So: 4x4 = 16 threads per threadgroup, chosen because the interleaved A/B (the only order-bias-free comparison) put it ~1.7 ms (about 3.6%) faster than 2x2, and both larger sizes (8x8, 16x16) were measurably slower.

Round-3 threadgroup sweep settled on 4 threads per threadgroup (TG4, i.e. threads_per_threadgroup = 4 in the dispatch), keeping the round-2 value.

How I know: the first sweep measured the candidate sizes in blocks (all runs of one size, then all of the next) and appeared to favour 2 threads per group, but that ordering coincided with a slow/fast drift in the session, so I re-ran the A/B with the two configurations strictly interleaved run-by-run in the same session on scene-default.json at 512x512/64spp with --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1. Interleaved, TG4 measured 45.3 ms best render_ms versus 47.0 ms for TG2 (about 3.6% faster), so TG2 was discarded as slot-order bias and TG4 was kept. That entry is recorded in my working memory under 'threadgroup: TG4 kept' with evidence from history messages 275-280.

Side note from the same session, for context only (no action taken): the 4-wide BVH experiment (128-byte nodes, 4 inline children, tree depth 8 vs 16) renders correctly but measures no faster than the current 2-wide wide1 tree (44.2-47.2 ms vs 44.7-49.8 ms across four interleaved reps), so it is not being adopted.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did not give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it.

How I know:
1. The first leaf2 measurement looked like a big win (33.5 ms vs ~50 ms) but it was a bug: the leaf payload carried only the first triangle index, so the second triangle of every leaf was never intersected. That build's RMSE against the frozen reference was 0.79 vs the baseline 0.476 — i.e. it was fast because it dropped geometry.
2. After fixing it (both triangles tested, leaf bounds merged), the same-session A/B was a wash against the round-2 build: 49.8 ms vs 49.7 ms best at 512x512/64spp.
3. It also lost to the layout pathtracer/ actually uses now: 64-byte wide nodes with one triangle per leaf (leaf triangles take no node slot, payload = triangle index, so per-triangle bounds and closest-hit tie behaviour are preserved) measured 44.3-46.4 ms in the same sessions.

So pathtracer/ keeps wide leaf-1. Consistent with that finding, the round-3 4-wide node variant (128B nodes, depth 8 vs 16, still one triangle per leaf) also failed to beat wide leaf-1 in a 4-rep interleaved A/B (W4 best 44.2-47.2 vs W1 44.7-49.8, no >=3% win), so wider leaves/nodes are not the lever here; I am moving on to shadow-ray/NEE cost cuts and register-pressure work.
